title: Whatsoever things are true (Philippians 4:8)
hook: think on whatever is true, modest, just, holy, lovely

segments.voice: Yesterday, rejoice in the Lord always, and peace standing guard. Your line was the lord is nigh. Which worry did you turn into a request? Day five hundred ninety.

Scroll back through what you looked at yesterday. Not to judge it. Just to notice what filled your head. The headlines. The arguments. The videos. The things you checked three times. Whatever gets in, stays a while and moves the furniture around. Paul seems to have known this long before screens. Near the end of his letter to Philippi, after rejoicing and peace, he gives his friends a list. Not of things to do. Of things to think about.
screen: `WHAT FILLED YOUR HEAD YESTERDAY?` → `WHAT GETS IN, STAYS.` → `A LIST OF THINGS TO THINK ABOUT.`

segments.voice: "For the rest, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever modest, whatsoever just, whatsoever holy, whatsoever lovely, whatsoever of good fame, if there be any virtue, if any praise of discipline, think on these things." Eight items. Some are familiar church words: just, holy. But others sound less like church and more like the Greek philosophers' schools. Virtue, aretē, was one of their great words: excellence. Lovely means lovable, winning, the kind of thing people are drawn to. Of good fame means well spoken of. Paul is reaching into the best of the wider culture and saying: that too. Whatever is true, wherever you find it. Then the verb: think on these things. The Greek word is logizesthe, a counting word, used for reckoning accounts. Take stock of these. Add them up. Dwell on them on purpose. Christian thinkers took this openness seriously. Justin Martyr wrote that whatever had been rightly said by anyone belongs to Christians. Centuries later, Thomas Aquinas read Aristotle with great care. And Paul ties the list to a promise in the next verse: do the things you've learned and seen, and the God of peace will be with you. This isn't about ignoring the hard news. Paul is in prison while he writes it. It's about choosing what you let settle in the mind, and what you leave at the door.
screen: `EIGHT THINGS TO THINK ON.` · `ARETĒ: THE PHILOSOPHERS' WORD.` · `THINK: RECKON, TAKE STOCK.` · `WHATEVER IS TRUE, WHEREVER FOUND.` · then, large: `WHATSOEVER THINGS ARE TRUE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: fill the room with one good thing. Settle, and breathe. Choose one thing from Paul's list. Something true you learned recently. Something just you saw someone do. Something lovely: a face, a song, the light this morning. Hold it in your mind on purpose. When your thoughts drift to a worry or an argument, notice, and gently bring them back. Turn the good thing over. Look at it from another side. If you pray, you can thank God for it. If you don't, simply let it stay, and let it take up room. The bell holds the time.
Whatsoever things are true. Paul's list of eight things worth thinking about: true, modest, just, holy, lovely, of good fame, virtue, praise. Today's word.
Your line: think on these. Today, before you open the news or a feed, think on one good thing for one full minute. Day five hundred ninety.

howItsDone: Catholic spiritual writers encourage guarding the imagination and filling the mind with good things through spiritual reading, sacred art and music; Philippians 4:8 is often quoted in that advice.

fork.setup: you're Paul, writing to friends who live in a pagan city full of philosophers. what do you say about the good things in their culture?
options: whatever is true, just, lovely, think on these things.
only scripture is worth thinking about.
fork.reveal: "whatsoever things are true... if there be any virtue... think on these things." he even uses the philosophers' word for virtue.

original.note: Greek: virtue, excellence; a word of the philosophers' schools, in Philippians 4:8.

trapdoor: what it means: choose on purpose what you dwell on: whatever is true, just, holy and lovely, wherever it's found.
what a scholar hears: aretē, the philosophers' excellence; prosphilēs, lovable; logizesthe, an accountant's verb.

sources.quoted: For the rest, brethren, whatsoever things are true, whatsoever modest, whatsoever just, whatsoever holy, whatsoever lovely, whatsoever of good fame, if there be any virtue, if any praise of discipline, think on these things.

notes: aretē appears only here in Paul's letters; prosphilēs only here in the New Testament. Confirm.
logizomai as an accounting/reckoning verb. Confirm.
Justin Martyr, Second Apology 13: 'whatever things were rightly said among all men are the property of us Christians'. Paraphrased. Confirm.
Aquinas's use of Aristotle: general statement.
